summary: Describes how to detect NAT devices between IPsec hosts and how to negotiate UDP encapsulation of IPsec packets through them in the Internet Key Exchange (IKE).

plainLanguage.summary:
A network address translation device, or NAT, rewrites the addresses in packets as they pass through, so the outside world sees a different address from the one the sender used. That breaks IPsec, which checksums and protects the address it was given.

RFC 3947 makes the two peers notice this for themselves. During the first phase of the key exchange, each side sends a hash of its own address and port. If the hashes match on both sides, no translation happened. If they do not, the peers know a NAT is in the way and agree to send their protected traffic inside a UDP packet.

questions: how does ipsec work behind nat
why does ipsec use udp port 4500
subtitle: How two IPsec peers notice a NAT in the way and agree to send their traffic through it.

tldr.problem: IPsec packets carry their own address information, and a network address translation device in the middle rewrites that address without telling either end. The security association then breaks, and there was no agreed way for the two peers to find out that translation had happened or to work around it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3947 adds two IKE payloads to the key exchange. Each end hashes its own addresses and ports and sends the hashes; if they do not match, a NAT is present. The initiator then moves to UDP port 4500 and Quick Mode agrees whether to wrap the traffic in UDP.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from January 2005 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It also warns that shared keys across a NAT are not recommended, and that the discovery payloads are not themselves authenticated.

today: RFC 3947 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2005. It has not been obsoleted or updated. Together with RFC 3948 it is the unconditionally compliant solution to the requirements in RFC 3715, and the port it registers, 4500, is the one IPsec uses for NAT traversal.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document is split into two parts. The first describes what is needed in IKE Phase 1 for NAT-Traversal support. This includes detecting whether the other end supports NAT-Traversal, and detecting whether there is one or more NATs between the peers.

The second part describes how to negotiate the use of UDP encapsulated IPsec packets in IKE's Quick Mode. It also describes how to transmit the original source and destination addresses to the peer, if required. These addresses are used in transport mode to update the TCP/IP checksums incrementally so that they will match after the NAT transform, because the NAT cannot do this, as the TCP/IP checksum is inside the UDP encapsulated IPsec packet.

RFC 3948 describes the details of UDP encapsulation and RFC 3715 provides background information and motivation for NAT-Traversal in general. In combination with RFC 3948, this document represents an unconditionally compliant solution to the requirements defined by RFC 3715.

In the basic scenario for this document, the initiator is behind a NAT and the responder has a fixed static IP address. The protocol that is defined works even if both ends are behind a NAT, but the process of how to locate the other end is out of the scope of this document. In one scenario the responder is behind a static host NAT, with only one responder per IP, as there is no way to use any destination ports other than 500 or 4500, so it is known by the configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The document answers three questions in order: does the other end understand NAT traversal, is there a NAT in between, and should the protected traffic be wrapped in UDP.

sections.title: Phase 1: Detecting NAT
sections.content:
The detection of support for NAT-Traversal and the detection of a NAT along the path between the two IKE peers occurs in IKE Phase 1. The NAT may change the IKE UDP source port, and recipients must be able to process IKE packets whose source port is different from 500. The NAT does not have to change the source port if only one IPsec host is behind the NAT, or if, for the first IPsec host, the NAT can keep port 500 and will only change the port number for later connections.

Recipients must reply back to the source address from the packet. This means that when the original responder is doing rekeying or sending notifications to the original initiator, it must send the packets using the same set of port and IP numbers used when the IKE security association was last used. For example, when the initiator sends a packet with source and destination port 500, the NAT may change it to a packet with source port 12312 and destination port 500. The responder must be able to process that packet, and must reply with a packet whose source port is 500 and destination port 12312, which the NAT will then translate to source port 500 and destination port 500.

The NAT-Traversal capability of the remote host is determined by an exchange of vendor ID payloads. In the first two messages of Phase 1, the vendor ID payload for this specification must be sent if supported, and it must be received by both sides, for the NAT-Traversal probe to continue. The content of the payload is the MD5 hash of the string RFC 3947, whose exact content in hex is 4a131c81070358455c5728f20e95452f.

The NAT-D payload not only detects the presence of a NAT between the two IKE peers, but also detects where the NAT is. The location matters, because the keepalives have to initiate from the peer behind the NAT. To detect NAT, the peers have to detect whether the IP address or the port changes along the path. This is done by sending the hashes of the IP addresses and ports of both peers from each end to the other. If both ends calculate those hashes and get the same result, they know there is no NAT between. If the hashes do not match, somebody has translated the address or port, and NAT-Traversal has to be used to get the IPsec packets through.

If the sender does not know its own IP address, for instance because it has multiple interfaces and does not know which address is used to route the packet out, it can include multiple local hashes as separate NAT-D payloads. In that case NAT is detected if and only if none of the hashes match. The hashes are sent as a series of NAT-D payloads, each containing one hash; in the normal case there are only two. They are included in the third and fourth packets of Main Mode, and in the second and third packets in Aggressive Mode.

The payload type for the NAT discovery payload is 20. The hash is calculated as HASH = HASH(CKY-I | CKY-R | IP | Port), using the negotiated hash algorithm, with all data inside the hash in network byte-order. The IP is 4 octets for an IPv4 address and 16 octets for an IPv6 address, and the port number is encoded as a 2 octet number in network byte-order. The first NAT-D payload contains the remote end's IP address and port, that is the destination address of the UDP packet, and the remaining NAT-D payloads contain possible local-end IP addresses and ports, that is all possible source addresses of the UDP packet.

If there is no NAT between the peers, the first NAT-D payload received should match one of the local NAT-D payloads, and one of the other NAT-D payloads must match the remote end's IP address and port. If the first check fails, meaning the first NAT-D payload does not match any of the local IP addresses and ports, there is dynamic NAT between the peers and this end should start sending keepalives, because this end is behind the NAT. The initiator and responder cookies are added to the hash to make precomputation attacks on the IP address and port impossible.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each side works out a fingerprint of its own address and port and sends it over. If the fingerprints the two sides compute for each other are the same, nothing was changed on the way. If they differ, something rewrote the address, and that something is a NAT.

The cookies are mixed into the fingerprint so that someone watching the exchange cannot work out the addresses by trying guesses ahead of time.

sections.title: Changing to New Ports
sections.content:
IPsec-aware NATs can cause problems. Some NATs will not change the IKE source port 500 even if there are multiple clients behind the NAT, and they can also use IKE cookies to demultiplex traffic instead of using the source port. Both are problematic for generic NAT transparency, as it is difficult for IKE to discover the capabilities of the NAT. The best approach is simply to move the IKE traffic off port 500 as soon as possible, to avoid any IPsec-aware NAT special casing.

Take the common case of the initiator behind the NAT. The initiator must quickly change to port 4500 once the NAT has been detected, to minimize the window of IPsec-aware NAT problems. In Main Mode, the initiator must change ports when sending the ID payload if there is NAT between the hosts, and must set both UDP source and destination ports to 4500. All subsequent packets sent to this peer, including informational notifications, must be sent on port 4500. In addition, the IKE data must be prepended with a non-ESP marker allowing for demultiplexing of traffic, as defined in RFC 3948.

When the responder gets this packet, the usual decryption and processing of the payloads is performed. If these are successful, the responder must update its local state so that all subsequent packets to the peer use the new port, and possibly the new IP address obtained from the incoming valid packet. The port will generally be different, as the NAT maps UDP(500,500) to UDP(X,500) and UDP(4500,4500) to UDP(Y,4500). The IP address will seldom differ from the pre-changed IP address. The responder must respond with all subsequent IKE packets to this peer by using UDP(4500,Y).

Similarly, if the responder has to rekey the Phase 1 security association, the rekey negotiation must be started by using UDP(4500,Y). Any implementation that supports NAT traversal must support negotiations that begin on port 4500, and if a negotiation starts on port 4500 then it does not need to change anywhere else in the exchange.

Once the port change has occurred, a packet received on port 500 is old. If it is an informational packet it may be processed if local policy allows. If it is a Main Mode or an Aggressive Mode packet with the same cookies as previous packets, it should be discarded. If it is a new Main Mode or Aggressive exchange, it is processed normally, since the other end might have rebooted.

If support for NAT-Traversal is enabled, the port in the ID payload in Main Mode or Aggressive Mode must be set to 0. The most common case for the responder behind a NAT is that the NAT is doing one-to-one address translation; in that case the initiator still changes both ports to 4500 and the responder uses the same algorithm, although Y will equal 4500 since no port translation is happening.

A different port change case involves out-of-band discovery of the ports to use, and those discovery methods are out of the scope of the document. If the responder is behind a port translating NAT and the initiator needs to contact it first, the initiator has to determine which ports to use, usually by contacting some other server. Once the initiator knows which ports to use to traverse the NAT, generally something like UDP(Z,4500), it initiates using these ports. The first keepalive timer starts after the change to the new port, and no keepalives are sent to port 500.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the NAT has been spotted, the initiator stops using the standard IKE port and moves both its ports to 4500, wrapping the IKE message in four extra bytes so a receiver can tell it apart from protected traffic. The responder notes the new port and uses it from then on.

sections.title: Quick Mode
sections.content:
After Phase 1, both ends know whether there is a NAT present between them. The final decision of using NAT-Traversal is left to Quick Mode. The use of NAT-Traversal is negotiated inside the SA payloads of Quick Mode. In Quick Mode, both ends can also send the original addresses of the IPsec packets, in the case of transport mode, to the other end so that each can fix the TCP/IP checksum field after the NAT transformation.

The negotiation of NAT-Traversal happens by adding two new encapsulation modes, UDP-Encapsulated-Tunnel with the value 3 and UDP-Encapsulated-Transport with the value 4. It is not normally useful to propose both a normal tunnel or transport mode and the UDP-Encapsulated modes. UDP encapsulation is required to fix the inability of NATs to handle traffic that is not UDP or TCP. If there is a NAT box between hosts, normal tunnel or transport encapsulations may not work, and in that case UDP encapsulation should be used. If there is no NAT box between, there is no point in wasting bandwidth by adding UDP encapsulation of packets, so it should not be used. The initiator should not include both a normal tunnel or transport mode and a UDP-Encapsulated-Tunnel or UDP-Encapsulated-Transport in its proposals.

To perform incremental TCP checksum updates, both peers may need to know the original IP addresses used by their peers when those peers constructed the packet. For the initiator, the original Initiator address is defined to be the Initiator's IP address and the original Responder address is defined to be the perceived peer's IP address. For the responder, the original Initiator address is defined to be the perceived peer's address and the original Responder address is defined to be the Responder's IP address.

The original addresses are sent using NAT-OA, NAT Original Address, payloads. The Initiator NAT-OA payload is first and the Responder NAT-OA payload is second. In the example where the initiator is behind a NAT talking to a publicly available responder, with addresses Iaddr, Raddr and NatPub, the initiator sends NAT-OAi equal to Iaddr and NAT-OAr equal to Raddr, and the responder sends NAT-OAi equal to NATPub and NAT-OAr equal to Raddr. With two NATs in between, the initiator sends NAT-OAi equal to Iaddr and NAT-OAr equal to Nat2Pub, and the responder sends NAT-OAi equal to Nat1Pub and NAT-OAr equal to Raddr.

In the case of transport mode, both ends must send both original Initiator and Responder addresses to the other end. For tunnel mode, both ends should not send original addresses. The NAT-OA payloads are sent inside the first and second packets of Quick Mode. The initiator must send the payloads if it proposes any UDP-Encapsulated-Transport mode, and the responder must send the payload only if it selected UDP-Encapsulated-Transport mode. It is possible for the initiator to send the NAT-OA payload but propose both UDP-Encapsulated transport and tunnel mode; the responder then selects the tunnel mode and does not send the NAT-OA payload back.

The payload type for the NAT original address payload is 21. The ID type is defined in RFC 2407, and only the ID_IPV4_ADDR and ID_IPV6_ADDR types are allowed. The two reserved fields after the ID Type must be zero.
sections.plainLanguage:
The first phase only says whether a NAT is there. The second phase decides what to do about it. Two new encapsulation modes are offered, one for tunnelled traffic and one for transport mode, and the choice is made in the same exchange that sets up the protected traffic.

In transport mode the peers also swap the addresses each originally used, because the checksum inside the protected packet still refers to the old address.

sections.title: Initial Contact Notifications
sections.content: The source IP and port address of the INITIAL-CONTACT notification for the host behind NAT are not meaningful, because the NAT can change them, so the IP and port numbers must not be used to determine which IKE and IPsec security associations to remove. The ID payload sent from the other end should be used instead. When an INITIAL-CONTACT notification is received from the other end, the receiving end should remove all the security associations associated with the same ID payload.
sections.plainLanguage: When a peer says it is closing down, the address it wrote in the message may be the NAT's address rather than its own. The peer identity in the ID payload is the reliable way to match the notification to the right connections.

sections.title: Recovering from Expiring NAT Mappings
sections.content:
There are cases where a NAT box decides to remove mappings that are still alive, for example when the keepalive interval is too long, or when the NAT box is rebooted. To recover from this, ends that are not behind NAT should use the last valid UDP encapsulated IKE or IPsec packet from the other end to determine which IP and port addresses should be used. The host behind dynamic NAT must not do this, as otherwise it opens a denial of service attack possibility, because the IP address or port of the other host will not change, it not being behind NAT.

Keepalives cannot be used for these purposes, as they are not authenticated, but any IKE authenticated IKE packet or ESP packet can be used to detect whether the IP address or the port has changed.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT can forget a mapping that is still in use. The end that has a fixed address can work out the new one from the last packet it received, but the end behind the NAT must not, because an attacker could use that to redirect its traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document lists several observations about the effects of NAT-Traversal and about whether or not those effects matter.

IKE probes reveal NAT-Traversal support to anyone watching the traffic, but disclosing that NAT-Traversal is supported does not introduce new vulnerabilities. The value of authentication mechanisms based on IP addresses disappears once NATs are in the picture. This is not necessarily a bad thing, since for any real security authentication measures other than IP addresses should be used. It means that authentication with pre-shared keys cannot be used in Main Mode without using group-shared keys for everybody behind the NAT box. Using group shared keys is a huge risk, because it allows anyone in the group to authenticate to any other party and claim to be anybody in the group, for example a normal user impersonating a VPN gateway and acting as a man in the middle. Use of group-shared keys is not recommended.

As the internal address space is only 32 bits and is usually very sparse, it might be possible for an attacker to find out the internal address used behind the NAT box by trying all possible IP addresses to find the matching hash. The port numbers are normally fixed to 500 and the cookies can be extracted from the packet, which limits the hash calculations to 2^32. If an educated guess of the private address space is made, the number of hash calculations needed falls to 2^24 plus twice 2^16.

Neither NAT-D payloads nor Vendor ID payloads are authenticated in Main Mode or in Aggressive Mode, so an attacker can remove them, modify them or add them. By removing or adding them, the attacker can cause denial of service attacks. By modifying the NAT-D packets, the attacker can cause both ends to use UDP-Encapsulated modes instead of directly using tunnel or transport mode, thus wasting some bandwidth.

Sending the original source address in Quick Mode reveals the internal IP address behind the NAT to the other end. In that case the two ends have already authenticated each other, and sending the original source address is only needed in transport mode.

Updating the IKE and ESP UDP encapsulation IP addresses and ports for each valid authenticated packet can cause denial of service if an attacker can listen to all the traffic in the network, change the order of the packets, and inject new packets before the packet already seen. The attacker can take an authenticated packet from the host behind the NAT, change its UDP source or destination ports or IP addresses, and send it out to the other end before the real packet reaches it. The host not behind the NAT will then update its address and port mapping and send further traffic to the wrong host or port. The situation is fixed immediately when the attacker stops modifying the packets, as the first real packet will fix it. Implementations should audit the event every time the mapping is changed, as it should not happen that often.
sections.plainLanguage: Two risks stand out. The hashes can be tampered with before they are authenticated, so an attacker can force the UDP mode or cut the connection. And the discovery handshake can leak the internal address to anyone who tries enough guesses.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document contains two new magic numbers allocated from the existing IANA registry for IPsec and renames an existing registered port, 4500. It also defines two new payload types for IKE.

The following new items were added to the ISAKMP Identifiers Encapsulation Mode registry: UDP-Encapsulated-Tunnel with the value 3 and UDP-Encapsulated-Transport with the value 4. In the registered port registry, the keyword ipsec-nat-t was registered with the decimal value 4500 for both TCP and UDP, with the description IPsec NAT-Traversal.

Two new IKE payload numbers were added to the Next Payload Types registry: NAT-D with the value 20, the NAT Discovery Payload, and NAT-OA with the value 21, the NAT Original Address Payload.
sections.plainLanguage: Three registry entries: two new IKE payload types, two new encapsulation modes, and the port number 4500 for IPsec NAT traversal.

viz.caption: When to use the UDP-encapsulated modes

items.title: Use them when there is a NAT
items.text: If a NAT box sits between the hosts, normal tunnel or transport encapsulations may not work, so UDP encapsulation should be used.

items.title: Skip them when there is no NAT
items.text: If there is no NAT box between the hosts, there is no point in wasting bandwidth by adding UDP encapsulation of packets.

items.title: Do not offer both
items.text: The initiator should not include both a normal tunnel or transport mode and a UDP-encapsulated mode in its proposals.

items.title: Why UDP is needed
items.text: UDP encapsulation is required to fix the inability of NATs to handle traffic that is not UDP or TCP.
